title: infrastructure-devops-security
universal_lens: The operational state space of a software system is modeled as a constrained Markov Decision Process. Deployment gates and security postures act as boundary conditions on the transition kernel, while readiness scorecards define a Lyapunov function ensuring asymptotic stability against unverified production mutations.
gsi_mapping: GSI treats launch-readiness scorecards as posterior probability distributions over system reliability. Unverified P0 data acts as high-variance noise; conformal prediction intervals are constructed around test evidence to bound the epistemic uncertainty of deployment outcomes before committing to live revenue streams.
gse_mapping: GSE maps the Definition of Ready and Done to strict state-transition operators in a finite automaton. A build card transitions from 'queued' to 'shipped' only if it satisfies the logical conjunction of QA evidence, compliance review, and rollback plan verification.

primitives.name: Deployment Gate Operator
primitives.verbatim_quote: # Infrastructure / DevOps / Security As of: 2026-06-09 ## Mission Owns CI, deployment gates, secrets, auth/admin controls, rollback, and security posture.
primitives.symbol_and_unit_ledger: Gate: Boolean (Pass/Fail); Secrets: Encrypted String; Rollback: Inverse Transition Function
primitives.assumptions: System transitions are discrete and require explicit authorization vectors to proceed.
primitives.breakdown_regime: Singularity occurs when gate enforcement fails (boolean collapse), allowing unauthorized state mutations or secret leakage into the public domain.

layer2.mapping: Isomorphic to GSE's constraint satisfaction layer where deployment gates map directly to pre-condition checks for valid state transitions.
layer2.telemetry: Gate pass/fail rate, number of blocked deployments, and time-to-rollback.

primitives.name: Readiness Lyapunov Function
primitives.verbatim_quote: ## Owned Metrics Readiness score, blocker count, test evidence, customer impact, revenue/trust/support metrics relevant to the department.
primitives.symbol_and_unit_ledger: Readiness Score: Dimensionless [0,1]; Blocker Count: Integer; Test Evidence: Binary Vector
primitives.assumptions: The readiness score monotonically decreases with increasing blocker counts and missing test evidence.
primitives.breakdown_regime: Breakdown occurs when the metric becomes decoupled from actual production stability (metric gaming), leading to false-positive launch approvals.

layer2.mapping: Maps to GSI's Bayesian confidence scoring, where readiness metrics serve as priors for estimating the probability of a successful, incident-free launch.
layer2.telemetry: Delta in readiness score per sprint, correlation between test coverage and post-launch P0 incidents.

primitives.name: Escalation Threshold
primitives.verbatim_quote: ## Escalation Rules Escalate legal/compliance, deploy, production data, payments, live affiliate, method leakage, or P0 data accuracy problems immediately.
primitives.symbol_and_unit_ledger: Severity: Enum (P0, P1, ...); Escalation Time: Seconds; Domain: Categorical Set
primitives.assumptions: Certain classes of errors (e.g., P0 data accuracy, payments) possess infinite cost and require immediate halting of standard workflows.
primitives.breakdown_regime: Failure regime when escalation latency exceeds the mean time to irreversible damage (e.g., financial loss or regulatory breach).

layer2.mapping: Isomorphic to GSE's emergency stop protocols, mapping critical failure states directly to synchronous interrupt handlers that bypass standard queuing.
layer2.telemetry: Mean time to acknowledge (MTTA) for P0 events, frequency of compliance breaches.

These gates act as boolean filters on the input alphabet $\Sigma$ (build cards like BUILD-CMD-048). 

The 'Owned Metrics' (Quote 7) introduce a scalar field $V(q)$ over the state space, acting as a Lyapunov function. For the system to be considered stable (launch-ready), $V(q)$ must exceed a critical threshold, contingent upon the absence of 'Launch Blockers' (Quote 4). Blockers effectively prune the state space, rendering certain transitions invalid. 

Furthermore, the 'Escalation Rules' (Quote 12) define a subset of catastrophic states $Q_{crit} \subset Q$. If the system enters $Q_{crit}$ (e.g., P0 data accuracy failure), the standard transition dynamics are suspended, triggering an orthogonal interrupt handler. This dual-layer approach—continuous monitoring via readiness scores and discrete intervention via escalation rules—ensures robustness against both gradual degradation and sudden singularities. The 'Definition of Ready' (Quote 10) formalizes the pre-image of valid transitions, requiring a conjunction of ownership, test plans, and rollback strategies before $\delta$ can be invoked.

reasoning_traces.theory_of_mind: We model the 'Department Lead' and 'QA Reviewer' as rational agents operating under bounded rationality. Their objective function is to maximize execution speed while minimizing risk exposure. They interpret the 'Readiness Score' as a compressed signal of system health. Opposing agents, such as 'hidden production config' or 'stale docs', act as adversarial noise sources attempting to deceive these observers into approving invalid state transitions.
reasoning_traces.cross_layer_veto: A cross-layer veto is triggered if the 'Readiness Score' (Layer 1 metric) indicates green status, but the 'Real App Evidence' (Layer 2 ground truth) reveals a red state (e.g., DB auth failure). This anti-collinearity between reported metrics and empirical reality constitutes a critical singularity. The system must enforce a hard veto on any deployment gate if the correlation between test evidence and live clone verification drops below a defined tolerance threshold.
